name: PASK

paper.title: PASK: Toward Intent-Aware Proactive Agents with Long-Term Memory

construction.unit: three tiers: user profile, session workspace, global tree with episode leaves ⟨fine tag, content⟩
construction.kept_as: profile traits (summarized); session history in the context window; episodes extracted from finished sessions
construction.processing: workspace state tracked every step; after a session, candidate traits are extracted for the profile and new episodes are inserted as raw leaves under a buffer node

organization.structure: cache / main memory / external storage; the global memory is a bounded-depth rooted tree of tag nodes over episode leaves
organization.stores: user memory (system prompt), workspace memory (context window), global memory (tree + RAG; Redis-style hot state and object/vector-store persistence per §5)
organization.index: RAG over leaf content under the anchor node (retriever not named)

management.operations: time-decayed profile update with conflict resolution; lazy CompressAndMerge of a node's children once their count exceeds η_merge; depth capped at D_max
management.conflicts: ResolveConflict reinforces matching traits, overwrites decayed contradictions and discards low-confidence anomalies
management.forgetting: confidence decay of outdated preferences; obsolete information pruned during merges

retrieval.query: q_t built from the latest segment, the history, an LLM observation summary and salient entities
retrieval.candidates: coarse: tag of the anchor node reused from the previous step; fine: RAG over leaves under that anchor
retrieval.selection: MemLoader (trained Qwen3-4B) distills the evidence; the Demand Detector then replies or stays silent

use.context: user profile + workspace state + anchor tag + distilled RAG evidence
use.reasoning: memory is read only when the detector emits <full_assistance>; otherwise silence or a fast reply from context

classify.note: Index and candidate type are read from 'RAG' and the vector-store backend in §5; the retriever itself is not described. A trained detector decides whether to retrieve and a trained MemLoader distills what is kept.

stages.ingestion: A frontend (glasses, computer, phone) turns speech and vision into a stream of text segments; the detector reads one segment per step.
stages.construction: Within a session the workspace memory keeps the history and a tracked state; after the session, traits are extracted for the user profile and episodes become new leaves under a buffer node of the global tree.
stages.organization: User memory sits in the system prompt (reused via KV cache), workspace memory in the context window, and global memory in a rooted tree whose internal nodes hold semantic tags and whose leaves hold a fine tag and episodic content.
stages.update: Offline only: profile traits decay over time and conflicts are resolved; a node's children are compressed and merged once they exceed η_merge, and depth is capped at D_max.
stages.retrieval: Only on a <full_assistance> token: an LLM summarizes the recent context and entities into a query, the anchor node from the previous step supplies a coarse tag, and RAG searches only that node's leaves; MemLoader distills the result.
stages.answer: The Demand Detector (Qwen3-30B-A3B, SFT + RL) writes the proactive reply or stays silent, using the profile, workspace and distilled evidence.
stages.learning: Demand Detector and MemLoader are fine-tuned separately on 100k synthetic samples, then jointly with DAPO RL on 2K real sessions (rule + LLM-judge rewards). The memory store itself is not trained.

summary: Proactive assistant whose trained detector decides each turn whether to stay silent, answer from context, or load memory from a three-tier store (profile cache, session workspace, lazily merged global tree).
notes:
Memory is one of three parts (DD-MM-PAS); most of the paper is the IntentFlow demand detector and the LatentNeeds benchmark. The released code (eval/, bench/) covers the benchmark only: no Pask-MM tree, RAG or MemLoader. In the benchmark every model, IntentFlow included in the released results, sees the same precomputed session 'memory' summary. Paper lists no η_merge, D_max, top-k or retriever.
DESIGN: §3.1, §4.1-4.3, §5, §6.1; code eval/prompts.py, bench/02_build_turns.py.

sources.code_note: The official repo (latest commit d54646c5, 2026-04-18) releases the LatentNeeds-Bench pipeline, evaluation prompts and per-model result/score files, but no code for Pask-MM (tree, RAG, merge, MemLoader) or IntentFlow training. The memory figures therefore follow the paper only; the benchmark facts follow the code.

headline: Memory is read only when the trained detector asks for it; most turns are silence or a fast reply from context.
Global retrieval does not search the whole tree: it reuses the previous step's anchor node and runs RAG only under it.
The benchmark gives every model the same precomputed memory summary, so none of the reported numbers isolates Pask-MM.

units.role: stable user profile; the cache tier

fields.name: profile traits
fields.what: domain expertise, thresholds, behavioural priors, with confidence weights that decay

fields.name: history H_t
fields.what: the session's text segments so far, in the detector's context window

fields.name: state s_t, contexts g, l, trace i
fields.what: tracked session state and global/local session contexts

units.name: Global memory (M_global)
units.made_by: leaves inserted after each session, merged lazily

fields.name: internal node tag
fields.what: semantic tag abstracting the subtree; the anchor's tag is returned as coarse memory

fields.name: leaf ⟨t_m, c_m⟩
fields.what: fine-grained tag and episodic content extracted from a finished session

units.name: Benchmark memory field
units.role: what the evaluated models actually receive as memory
units.made_by: gpt-5-nano summary in the released pipeline

fields.name: memory
fields.what: 2-4 sentence (200-300 character) summary of all earlier 60-turn parts of the same recording; empty for the first part. A separate script (bench/03c_memory.py, not in run_pipeline.sh) can write a longer gpt-5.2 memory instead; the data file is not released, so which one the scored runs saw cannot be checked

write.how: each step updates the workspace state from the observation, history and time
after a session, candidate traits U′ are extracted; old traits decay with elapsed time and ResolveConflict reinforces, overwrites or discards
episodes from the finished session become raw leaves under a buffer node; ancestors are not recomputed
when a node's children exceed η_merge, CompressAndMerge deduplicates siblings and prunes obsolete items; depth is capped at D_max

read.how: an LLM agent writes an observation summary o_t and salient entities e_t; combined into q_t
reuse the node located at the previous step; its tag is the coarse event memory (no full-tree traversal)

read.scores: episodic content c_m of leaves under the anchor

read.how: MemLoader (Qwen3-4B-Instruct, SFT + RL) condenses the retrieved evidence
Demand Detector reads profile, workspace, anchor tag and distilled evidence; replies or returns nothing

answer_context.sees: user profile, workspace state, anchor tag and MemLoader-distilled evidence (paper); in the benchmark: scene, one memory summary and the full part history
answer_context.format: benchmark user message: "[Scene] ... [Memory from earlier conversation] ... [Conversation] speaker: text ... [Current turn] speaker: text" after a system prompt at one of three intervention levels
includes: all earlier turns of the 60-turn part
answer_context.note: The paper's runtime context (Eq. 9) cannot be checked in code; the benchmark prompt is what the released results use.

compression.what: benchmark memory summary vs the earlier conversation it replaces
compression.basis: Not reported in the paper. The released pipeline asks gpt-5-nano for 200-300 characters (max 200 tokens) over earlier turns, each cut to 200 characters.
Not reported: the paper gives no leaf counts, tree sizes or token budgets.

paper_vs_code.paper: IntentFlow keeps performance stable 'with Pask-MM' over long interactions
paper_vs_code.code: every model's prompt carries the same session memory summary produced by the data pipeline; no Pask-MM retrieval is run

paper_vs_code.paper: balanced average of demand and non-demand accuracy
paper_vs_code.code: the per-model best prompt level is chosen by pooled balanced accuracy; the released score files reproduce the table's Overall Avg. as the mean of the 10 subcategory averages

open_questions: No run removes or swaps the memory module, so the benchmark cannot show what Pask-MM adds; the stability claim rests on IntentFlow vs other models, all given the same summary.
IntentFlow is the fine-tuned model; its gain over its base (58.9 → 84.2) mixes intent training with anything memory-related.

glance.a: Three kinds: profile traits in the system prompt, the session history in the context window, and leaves in a global tree holding a fine tag and an episode.
As a cache / main memory / external storage hierarchy; the global tier is a rooted tree of semantic tags with a capped depth.
The workspace is updated every step; profile and tree are updated only after the session ends.
Only when the detector emits <full_assistance>; retrieval then searches the leaves under the previous step's anchor node.
Not in isolation. The benchmark gives every model one precomputed summary of earlier parts; long-term memory is shown only through case studies.

text: The detector emits one token per segment: stay silent, reply from context, or load memory.
Loading memory reuses the last anchor node's tag and runs RAG only under it; a small trained model distills the evidence before the detector replies.

discussion.takeaway: A proactive agent needs a fast gate that decides when to speak and when to load memory. PASK trains that gate (IntentFlow) and pairs it with a tiered memory, and reports the best balanced accuracy on its own LatentNeeds-Bench at the lowest latency.

claims.claim: A trained open model matches fast frontier models on latent-need detection.
claims.evidence: Balanced accuracy 84.2 vs 80.8 (Gemini-3-Flash), 77.2 (GPT-5-Mini); demand accuracy 83.1 vs 83.3 (Gemini-3-Flash). Table 1, §6.2

claims.claim: Training, not the base model, gives the gain.
Performance stays stable over long sessions with Pask-MM.
claims.evidence: 86.1 → 81.8 from turns 1-4 to 57-60 (−5.0%), vs −17.3% Gemini-3-Flash and −19.0% GPT-5-Mini. Table 3, §6.4
1.3-1.5 s per turn vs 3.2-4.4 s for Gemini-3-Flash. Table 4, §6.5.1

claims.claim: Long-term memory helps with background, knowledge and preferences.
claims.evidence: Case studies only, no metric. Fig. 9, §6.5.2

limits: The benefits of long-term memory are hard to measure in open-ended settings, so they are shown by case studies.
IntentFlow does not set a new ceiling; it trails Gemini-3-Flash on demand accuracy (83.1 vs 83.3) and in Work scenarios (84.8 vs 91.5).
Daily-life assistance is the hardest in the user study; deep intent understanding remains unsolved.
reading: The benchmark input gives all models the same scene description, a precomputed summary of earlier parts and the full 60-turn part history; none of the scored runs uses the global tree, RAG or MemLoader, so Table 1 and Table 3 measure the detector, not Pask-MM.
No memory ablation is reported; the multi-turn stability claim compares different models, not IntentFlow with and without memory.
The released code sets the judge to gpt-4.1-mini while the paper names GPT-5.2.
Each baseline is reported at its best of three prompt levels, while the released IntentFlow scores are from the neutral level only.
A reply on a no-demand turn counts as correct if the judge accepts it (score files label it fp_accepted), so No-Dem. accuracy is not simply staying silent.
Key memory settings (η_merge, D_max, top-k, retriever, what extracts traits and episodes) are not given anywhere.

abstract.text: PASK studies proactive assistants that listen to a live stream and must decide, turn by turn, whether and how to help without being asked. It proposes a three-part design: demand detection, memory modelling and an always-on agent system. Demand detection is done by IntentFlow, a Qwen3-30B-A3B model trained with SFT and RL that emits a silence, fast-reply or memory-backed token; memory is split into a user profile, a session workspace and a lazily merged global tree searched by RAG. On a new real-world benchmark, LatentNeeds-Bench, IntentFlow reaches the best balanced accuracy among the tested models at the lowest latency.
